chunks.text: Cassia javanica, called Java cassia, pink shower, apple blossom tree or rainbow shower tree, is a Fabaceae-family tree native to a broad arc from Assam through southern China and the Malesian region to Queensland, Australia, and introduced to India, Hawaii, Sri Lanka and parts of tropical Africa and America. It is fast-growing and reaches 25-40 m, with paripinnate leaves of about a dozen leaflet pairs and open clusters of pale pink to crimson flowers with yellow stamens; towards the end of the flowering season the ground beneath a mature tree is often carpeted pink with fallen petals. Flowering timing varies by region (April-May in India, February-April in Thailand, October-December with dry-season fruiting in East Java), and the species is polymorphic enough that Plants of the World Online recognises seven subspecies. Beyond its value as a street and park shade tree, it has a documented place in traditional medicine as a substitute for Cassia fistula in treating constipation, colic and urinary disorders, its bark is used in Ayurvedic antidiabetic preparations and in leather tanning, and its timber is worked into furniture and general construction. In Thailand it is one of the Nine Auspicious Trees, believed to bring good fortune, and it is the provincial flower of Chainat Province; in the Philippines, the popular 'Palawan cherry blossom' sold under this group's name is often a different, non-native Cassia hybrid rather than the true native subspecies pubiflora.

chunks.source: NParks Singapore — Flora & Fauna Web (Cassia javanica subsp. nodosa, 'Pink Cassia')
chunks.text: Singapore's National Parks Board profiles the widely planted pink-flowered form of this species as Cassia javanica subsp. nodosa, native to Indonesia, Peninsular Malaysia and Thailand, growing 10-20 m tall with deciduous compound leaves of five to twelve leaflet pairs and cylindrical seed pods 30-70 cm long that blacken as they ripen. NParks classes it as an ornamental tree suited to parks, gardens and smaller residential plots, grown in full sun on moist, well-drained soil, and notes that its flowers make it an effective butterfly-attracting species — useful information for a park setting where biodiversity value matters alongside visual appeal. The entry is a reminder that common names in this group are applied loosely: 'pink cassia', 'apple-blossom cassia' and 'Javanese cassia' are all used for subsp. nodosa specifically, while the species as a whole (including other subspecies) carries a wider native range from Assam to southern China. NParks' profile, like most official plant database entries, stops short of endorsing medicinal use and advises consulting a physician rather than relying on folk applications.
